p: Yes. We work with them very closely, and we’ve worked with them to do blitz’s in particular in areas we get these complaints, and we try to work with them to go back over a period of time so that it’s not just they got to take it once and then it goes away. But we really try to focus it for a while, and then we work with the Trucking Association and others to provide information on where it is legal, because we do understand that there is a need, and we want to make sure that we’re doing both the enforcement and the providing alternatives.
Okay, great. Thank you.

Thank you. Last set of questions. Oh, I think I see my former staffer in the audience. Milo, how you doing? Nice to see you. I’m going to turn it to just a few questions. Resurfacing Fifth Avenue– the Executive Plan includes additional city funds of $453,000 in fiscal 2026 only

to resurface Fifth Avenue. What will this funding be used for? Please be specific.

So, ahead of the capital project that’s happening on Fifth Avenue, we wanted to make sure that the surface has a good riding surface ahead of FIFA and other events. So, that is why there was specific funding added for expense resurfacing of Fifth Avenue.
If it’s just resurfacing, why isn’t this capitally eligible?
So, resurfacing by itself is capitally eligible, Chair, but because a capital project is coming up, we didn’t want to mess with the capital eligibility of the larger Fifth Avenue project.
If we paved it with capital funds, it would basically preclude us from coming back to do the capital streetscape project for a certain amount of time and we didn’t want to preclude it.

Okay. Regarding public realm, $6.4 million in city funding was baselined starting in fiscal 27 for public realm programs. Will this funding just be used to support

open streets at its current level or will it be used to expand the program?

Yes. So, first, we’re very grateful that the funding was baselined. So we’re not going year to year anymore and not knowing what’s coming up. So, we think that’s a really important investment to us to be able to plan. And as the Commissioner said earlier, we do see the program growing. It’s bigger at this point this year than it was last year, and it’s not constrained by the money, right? We’ve always been able to do whatever has been needed even if we have to move some money around internally. So we’re committed to growing the program, and not just from a money perspective, but providing programming where it’s needed. We’ve been working a lot on process to make sure that partners get paid much faster. I think there’s– the money and the long-term planning enable us to be able to do much moe in terms of working closely with those partners.
So, fair to say it is expanding?
Yeah. We don’t turn anyone away because of money.
What other plaza programs will receive funding, if any?

So, we– you know, we are committed to expanding our plaza program and we have an applicant-based process for that every year, and as part of that we have our plaza equity funds, or sorry, our public space equity funds, because it goes beyond plazas now, and so we want to make sure that whoever has an idea for a plaza, we can work with them whether to test it short term as an open street, whether to eventually build it up capitally to provide ongoing maintenance support, this is something we’re very committed to as an agency.

And my last question is on street lights. In fiscal 2025 it took DOT an average of 5.3 calendar days to repair street lights which is a 20.5 percent increase from 4.4 days in fiscal 24 and 76 percent slower than the three days in fiscal 21. It took Con-Ed 22 calendar days on average to repair street lights, which is 17.6 percent slower than the 18.7 days in fiscal 2024, and 45.7 percent slower than the 50.1 days in fiscal 21. The MMR indicates that DOT delays were due to

weather-related outages and coordination issues with utilities during underground infrastructure work. No explanation of the Con-Ed performance decline was included. The Executive Plan has an additional $1.5 million in fiscal 26 only for the street light maintenance. What will this money go towards? Is money going towards already existing contracts for street light maintenance?
Chair, yes, it is.

So, this funding is going toward already existing contracts with the vendors is what it sounds like. I’m a little concerned about that. With this money– will this money be directly used to increase coordination times with Con-Ed?

So, we meet with Con-Ed very often. In fact, I met with them this week on various issues. We’re constantly talking with them, but what is happening with our street lighting system is that overall it’s pretty aged and we have– when ever we have a Con-Ed issues, oftentimes it has something to do with the underground conduit needing to be replaced and that

is not just changing a bulb, it’s more than a quick repair. So, you’re raising a valid issue. It is something that we are working on both internally with our contractors and with Con-Ed.

I mean between now and adoption, is there some way to add resources to focus in on increasing, you know, the coordination, because it’s something that we hear, you know, time on end. This is a basic and essential function of the department. If this funding is not being used to coordinate with Con-Ed or just speed up street light maintenance, you know, I then have to ask what is DOT doing differently? Because the current contracts and systems operations in place doesn’t seem to be working well.

Right. So, the coordination is not something that we need funding for. Again, it kind of comes back to the physical plant, the infrastructure itself, and we’re also looking at advancing some capital projects for larger areas in each borough where we know that the street lighting infrastructure is old and needs to be replaced in order to be reliable. So, that’s

kind of the area that we’re looking toward in the future.
And my last question– is there additional monies in the budget for updated street light infrastructure?

Yes, there is. We have received $331 million in order to replace every LED in the city and then also to provide sensors in every street light that will give us real time information on the functioning of that street light.
Thank you very much, Commissioner.
Thank you.

Okay. I think we are actually done for this portion with the Department of Transportation. So, thank you so much, Commissioner. Just want to give a special shout out. You have an amazing First Deputy Commissioner, Margaret, who is very helpful to a lot of us and has been. So, thank you so much. Just wanted to give you a shout out, but not that I don't like the rest of you guys, but you know what I mean. Thank you so much everyone.
Thank you, Council Members.
Okay. And we’re going to roll right into DCWP which is next. So, we’re just going to take a couple minutes to transition.
Keep it down, please. Quiet, please. We’re about to start. We’re about to resume. Please have a seat. At this time, please have a seat, please. Thank you very much for your kind cooperation.

Can I start? Oh, we’re good. Okay. Hello. Good afternoon everyone and welcome to the second FY 27 Executive Budget hearing for the day focusing on Department of Consumer and Worker Protection. Council Member Lee, I’m joined by our Speaker, Speaker Menin, as well as our Council Member Harvey Epstein, Chair of the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. I would like to recognize we’ve been joined by Deputy Speaker Williams, Council Member Krishnan, Banks, Wong, and Pierina Sanchez, and Council Member Schulman. So, welcome to our Commissioner Sam Levine and your team. Thank you all for joining us today to answer our questions. On May 12th, 2026, the administration

released the Executive Financial Plan for FY26 to FY30 with a proposed FY27 budget of $124.7 billion. The Department of Consumer and Worker Protections proposed FY27 budget of $78.4 million represents less than one percent of the administration’s proposed FY27 budget in the Executive Plan, and this is an increase of $3.7 million or five percent from the $74.7 million originally budgeted in the FY27 Preliminary Plan. This increase results from several options, mostly from the significant and sustained increase of 77 positions at DCWP in FY27, increasing to 181 positions in 2029. As of April 26th, DCWP’s budget headcount was 85 more than their fiscal 26 budgeted headcount. Further, the mayor announced plans to double the budget of DCWP in order to strengthen worker protections and enforcement. In addition, DCWP has 19.3 percent vacancy rate that makes it difficult to meet its operational demands, and we’re pleased to see that these additional funds were partially included in the plan. My questions will largely focus on the mayor’s campaign promise where he pledged to double the agency’s budget. Savings from OFE’s [sic] estimation of the financial literacy expansion, and the savings that we are

seeing from discontinuing the cloud migration program. And now, at this time, I will turn it over to Speaker Menin for her remarks.

Thank you so much, Chair Lee, and I really want to thank our Finance Chair for her great work in holding these hearings, and I want to thank our Consumer and Worker Protection Chair, Council Member Harvey Epstein, for his terrific work on chairing this committee. And I want to thank you, Commissioner and your team, for being here and to all the advocates that have taken time to participate in this budget process. So, this hearing, in particular, is very meaningful to me, as I had the honor of serving as Commissioner of this agency and as Chair of this committee and I’ve garnered a very deep appreciation over the very many years for the dedicated public servants who carry out this work each and every day. But those experiences also reinforce the importance of rigorous oversight and responsible fiscal management. Our responsibility today is to ensure that the fiscal year 2027 budget adequately equips the agency to meet its mission while delivering transparency, efficiency, and measurable outcomes for New Yorkers. The mayor

pledged to double DCWP’s budget during his campaign, recognizing that the agency needs greater funding to be successful. However, in the Executive Budget, the mayor pledged an additional $3.7 million to DCWP, bringing the agency’s total 2027 funding to $78.4 million under his proposal. We in the Council have consistently warned that insufficient funding could hamper DCWP’s ability to investigate complaints and enforce Local Laws. To ensure that the agency has the staffing and operational capacity needed to carry out responsibilities assigned through the Local Laws, the Council is asking for an additional $32 million for DCWP. I understand certainly that behind every single in the budget there is a real impact on our communities. As we review at the Council, we'll closely examine whether the proposed investments are sufficient to meet current and future needs, whether resources are being allocated equitably, and whether the agency has the staffing, infrastructure and operational support necessary to succeed. In particular, I’m concerned about whether the Department has sufficient staffing for its wide range of oversight and enforcement responsibilities, particularly on newer items that stem from Council

initiated laws covering for high vehicles driver deactivation, security guard minimum wages, protected time off, delivery worker laws, and other items. I just want to say, the Council has passed so many important bills in this regard, and so we really want to make sure that the agency then has the proper resources to enforce them, because we’ve done all this work to pass these laws, but if we don’t have the resources to enforce them, we’re not really getting the results that we need to do. So, we’ll also be looking carefully at how the administration plans to address ongoing challenges, improve service delivery and ensure that taxpayer dollars are being spent effectively and responsibly. New Yorkers deserve a government that is responsive, accountable, and capable of meeting the moment. Today’s hearing is an important opportunity to assess where progress is being made, where gaps remain, and where additional actions may be necessary in the future. I look forward to a productive discussion and working collaboratively to ensure that this agency has all the tools and support needed to serve the people of this city. And I’m now going to turn it over to Chair Epstein for his remarks.

I want to thank you, Chair Lee and Speaker Menin for your leadership on these issues. I know, especially Speaker Mening, you know, your familiarity with these issues both as a Commissioner and the Chair of this is really invaluable. I want to thank the Commissioner of DCWP for joining us today to talk about the Consumer Worker Protection budget for this upcoming fiscal year. You know, as we have heard already and the questions we’re talking about is around the additional positions that you’re hiring, the needs that the agency will have to ensure that it’s fully funded to make sure that the workers and the consumers in New York get the support that they need. You know, we really want to hear about the increased numbers in active workers, consumer protection laws that the Speaker mentioned, and if the proposed budget will ensure that they have enough staffing in place to make sure we follow those needs. You know, as my personal history, as well as the Speaker, we’re really uniquely able to understand these concerns. I see this history for New Yorkers. You know, I do want to thank you, Commissioner Levine, for being here, your Deputy Commissioner Elizabeth Wugon [sic], Chief

of Staff Carlos Ortiz, and General Counsel Michael Tiger for being here today. We really look forward to this active conversation where over the next to figure out– a few weeks– what our goals are together to ensure that the Committee and the staff and the Speaker and the Council make sure we have enough resources to ensure that you are getting done what you need for New Yorkers. I want to thank my team, the Legislative Division, Sarah Swain [sp?], Natalie Meltzer, my staff, Jackson Fisher Ward [sp?], Jenna Mien [sp?], and our Finance Division, Glen Maritole [sp?], Daniel Krup [sp?], and Chima Obicheri [sp?], who really put this together to make sure that we have a successful hearing. And I’ll turn it back over to Chair Lee.

Great. I also want to recognize we have been joined by Council Member Morano on Zoom, as well as Justin Sanchez. So, before we get started, really quickly just wanted to announce some logistics. So, as you all know, if you’ve heard me speak at other hearings, because of the crunch in timeline for our Executive Budget hearings, we’re going to do public testimony all on one day, Wednesday, June 10th, starting at 9:30 a.m.

so, please join us that day. We’re going to try to make it as fun as we can. So, Executive Budget hearings for the public testimony portion is Wednesday, June 10th, starting at 9:30 a.m. So please make sure to let folks know. And with that, I’ll turn it over to Committee Counsel to swear in the witnesses.
Good afternoon. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions? Commissioner Levine?
I do.
Deputy Commissioner Wagoner?
I do.
Chief of Staff Ortiz?
I do.
And General Counsel Tiger?
I do.
You may begin.

Well, thank you, Speaker Menin, Chair Lee, Chair Epstein, and members

of the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. I’m Sam Levine, Commissioner of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection. Today I’m joined by our General Counsel Michael Tiger, our Chief of Staff, Carlos Ortiz, and our Deputy Commissioner of the Office of Labor Policy and Standards, Elizabeth Wagoner. Thank you for the opportunity to be here today before this committee to testify on the work of our agency and our Executive Budget for fiscal year 2027. DCWP is the nation’s leading municipal enforcement agency charged with delivering economic justice. We leverage our authority to bring New Yorkers real economic relief and protect them from predatory, deceptive, and unconscionable practices that violate their rights as consumers and as workers. This includes pioneering cutting-edge protections such as the city’s Consumer Protection Law, Protected Time Off Law, Fair Work Week Law, and Delivery Worker Laws, including the minimum pay rate for delivery workers. Through licensing more than 45,000 businesses in over 45 industries, DCWP ensures fair competition and a level playing field for responsible small businesses that are integral to New York City’s vibrant communities. DCWP also provides

essential services such as free tax preparation for individuals and families as well as tax prep services for self-employed workers in small businesses, and one-on-one financial counseling to ensure New Yorkers keep more of what they earn and plan for their futures. Though it’s been just short of six months under my tenure, it’s been a privilege to serve as the Commissioner of DCWP, an agency that champions millions of consumers, workers, and families across the city day after day. Today I’ll provide the committee with an overview of the Executive Budget for FY27, the work of our agency, and our path forward in continuing to build a fairer and more affordable city for all New Yorkers under Mayor Mamdani’s administration. Starting with our budget. For FY27, DCWP’s Executive Budget is approximately $78.5 million with an active headcount of 409 and an authorized headcount of 561, the highest authorized headcount our agency has ever had. This is due in no small part to the advocacy of our partners, this council, and of course the immense support and recognition of our agency’s work by our mayor. Mayor Mamdani’s Executive Budget represents the single greatest investment in consumer and worker rights in

DCWP history. All told, DCWP will be receiving a total of 181 new lines, and $17.9 million in personnel services by FY29. THe breakdown is as follows: In FY27, DCWP will receive 77 lines and $4.3 million in personnel services. In FY28 we will receive 76 lines and $7.3 million in personnel services, and in FY29, we will receive 28 lines and the remaining $6.3 million in personnel services. The new lines we’ll be receiving in FY27 will be strategically deployed to immediately begin implementation of major new laws and much needed protections for New Yorkers. Going on to the important work we do. It has been just shy of six months since the start of my tenure and I’m beyond proud of what this agency has already accomplished under the Mamdani administration. Our team has been at the forefront of the administration implementing cutting-edge new mandates, aggressively pursuing new protections, and securing victory after victory for the people of New York. These range from our expedited– excuse me– expanded delivery worker laws including a minimum pay rate for grocery delivery workers and expanded protected time off law, and soon to come, deactivation protections for key workforces

and more licenses for our city street vendors. I also want to be sure to emphasize Chair Epstein’s much-needed legislation to address the student loan debt crisis in our city. Under Local Law 84, we will be expanding our critical financial empowerment center network by providing student loan debt services which would be essential for New Yorkers. In addition to the new laws and requirements, DCWP has also taken more proactive and innovative steps to strengthen protections for those who make our city run. Earlier this year, tasked with tackling deceptive and predatory practices under the Mayor’s Executive Orders, DCWP adopted the strongest prohibition on hotel junk fees in the United States. This rule protects both New Yorkers traveling outside the city and those visiting our city from unexpected and costly fees. With projected savings of up to $35 million a year for New Yorkers, and up to $31 million a year for visitors. We also proposed rules to ensure that consumers can easily cancel automatic renewals and subscriptions. Our Click to Cancel Rule is estimated to save New Yorkers up to $162.5 million a year, according to an analysis by the Roosevelt Institute. Lastly, we finalized the Shield Rule, a

debt collection rule that provides New Yorkers with the nation’s strongest protections against debt collector harassment. In addition to expanded protections under our rules, we also released the benchmarking report and a data-driven enforcement strategy for New York City’s Protected Time Off Law, leading and guiding the nation in education and compliance on a cornerstone workplace right. This work to further New Yorker’s rights will only continue as we proactively leverage our authority to pursue an ambition agenda delivering on the Mayor’s vision. While we have been working to implement and expand protections afforded to New Yorkers, we have also been fighting harder than ever before to vigorously enforce our laws, cracking down on predatory corporate practices to hold bad actors accountable. We started 2026 by launching a robust compliance blitz, sending notices to various industries, reminding them of their obligations under the law and the repercussions that arise from noncompliance. This past January, we exposed Uber and Doordash for deceptive design tricks that made it harder for consumers to tip delivery workers, driving down worker pay by more than half a billion dollars

in New York City alone. We have shown major corporations that there are consequences for violating our laws. We are actively seeking millions of penalties in restitution from numerous predatory businesses for exploiting and cheating New Yorkers. These efforts span across our work, delivering real results for consumers, workers, and small businesses alike. For example, we secured $5 million from three delivery apps for violations of the minimum pay rate, and more than half a million dollars for freelancers ripped off by the production company Splashlight [sp?]. In March, we announced a $1.5 million settlement with Dunkin and Taco Bell franchisees for violations of the Fair Work Week Law, securing economic justice and fairness for more than 760 workers. We took legal action against predatory businesses like Extra Space [sic], Radiant Solar, and Instant [sic] Recovery Corporation, seeking over tens of millions of dollars in penalties for deceptive and illegal schemes to raise costs for New Yorkers. We also went after major employment agencies, including CMP, Golden Rose, and Elanies [sp?] and won almost $1 million in restitution for individuals who face exploitation and violations of their rights by these

businesses. In April, we announced a settlement of more than $875,000 with Hungry Panda for violating New York City’s fee cap law in charging small immigrant-owned restaurants thousands of dollars in illegal junk fees, the first action our agency has ever brought under this authority. And most recently, the mayor announced our action against Honda of the Bronx, a used car dealer engaging in widespread deceptive practices. All of this work is a clear reminder that under this administration, there is zero tolerance for companies that violate the law, and that we will fight to bring justice to the New Yorkers that faced abuses. The numbers speak for themselves. Within the mayor’s first 100 days, we had already secured nearly $10 million for New Yorkers, and that number is only growing as we continue delivering real economic justice to consumers, workers, and small businesses across our city. This is just the beginning of a transformative era, and we look forward to continuing our relentless fight to bring accountability, affordability and economic justice to the people of New York. I thank you for the opportunity to testify today and DCWP’s commitment to championing consumers, workers and

families in this new era of economic justice for all New Yorkers. I would again like to express my gratitude to Mayor Mamdani, to Chair Epstein, to the Speaker, to Chair Lee, to members of this committee and to all of our partners in this room for the steadfast advocacy on our agency’s behalf. It really means the world. We are eager to continue our success delivering millions in real economic relief to countless New Yorkers and advancing Mayor Mamdani’s agenda for a fairer, more affordable New York City. I look forward to answering your questions.

Okay, great. Thank you very much. So, we appreciate the testimony today. I want to get a little bit more into the headcount, because I know you said this is the biggest investment that’s been made into DCWP. I think our finance team has some concerns about that assertion, because it’s our understanding that last year in terms of where the budget was, both with headcount and overall amount, that it actually was higher last year. So we sort of want to get into those numbers. I’m sure the Chair will get into that as well. Do you have any comments on that?

Sure. I’m happy to explain that, Madam Speaker. Last year’s budget was, you might say, inflated by the inclusion of the summer contract for city residents. That was budgeted at $12 million for FY26. Under the current plan, we are eliminating the program for city residents, effective in FY27. So, that’s going to reduce $12 million and then $14 million in FY27, $16 million in FY28, and we’re plowing that money into our enforcement work. So, if you look at our actual budget for enforcement, it’s growing significantly.

Okay. I guess what we want to get clarity on is you mentioned in your opening statement that the highest authorized headcount of 561, but your active headcount is 409 which is lower than 417 this past July. So, we want to understand that.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. We do have vacancies. We have a vacancy rate of 16 percent right now. So we have a lot of hiring to do in FY27. We have vacancies to fill. We have 77 new lines to hire, and I can tell you if you go onto our website right now, we have jobs posted. We’re already actively engaging in hiring.

And I would note, too, Speaker that our authorized headcount for fiscal year 26 was 483, but obviously with the Mayor’s investment for this fiscal year and moving into fiscal year 29, we’re looking at I think overall 40 percent increase in the headcount of the agency.
And how quickly do you think you’re going to be hiring?

We’re think we’re going to be on pace to hire– I don’t have month by month, Speaker, but we are going to be on pace to both close our current vacancies and hire the 77 through FY27. We're already moving.

So, the Council, as you know, is calling on the administration to allocate an additional $32 million for DCWP’s budget to meet the need of the numerous pieces of critical legislation on consumer and worker protection that the Council has passed in recent years. Do you feel that this additional funding would be sufficient to appropriately carry out the agency’s mission?

Well, I haven’t had a chance to look at the details of the Council’s proposal. I learned about it today. I greatly

appreciate the vote of confidence that you have placed in the agency. I know you have particular affection for DCWP as do I, and the vote of confidence by the committee. With respect to the Executive Budget, which I have looked at, we fell confident that with respect to the laws that the Council passed, the new mandates as you referenced Madam Speaker for our agency, that the 181 headcount that the Executive Budget authorized would be sufficient to meet our needs.
Okay. DCWP issue– well, let me just– before I move on from that. So, you’re saying that you do not need any additional funding beyond what is in the Executive Budget?
We always welcome more resources generally, and I know that the Council is considering new laws including with new responsibilities for DCWP–
[interposing] Right.

and I expect we’ll have follow-up conversations about new needs there. But with respect to the bills the Council’s passed and that are already being implemented, we worked

really closely with OMB and City Hall and we feel we have what we need.

Okay. Earned safe and sick leave time. So, I want to talk a little bit about that. So, DCWP issued compliance warnings to roughly 56,000 New York City employers following the implementation of the earned safe and sick time amendments. What percentage of those employers have achieved compliance and what enforcement actions have been taken against those that have not?

Well, I appreciate the question. We take a lot of pride in that warning blitz. I’m going to turn things over to my colleague to share a little more. But the goal of that was not to open investigations of all of those thousands of businesses. It’s two-fold. One, we wanted to make sure businesses understood their obligation. I don’t believe in gotcha [sic] enforcement. I believe in making sure businesses understand their obligations, workers understand their rights. That was the goal there. But also we wanted to make sure businesses knew that we were watching, that given the high volume of complaints over the years we’ve gotten about PTO, I wanted businesses to know that we took

violations really seriously. That’s why we followed up with warnings. That’s why we followed up with enforcement. With respect to the number of in compliance, I don’t think we’ve investigated every one of those businesses, but I’ll turn things over to my Deputy Commissioner to share more.

No, that’s– echoing everything the Commissioner said, and to generate that list, you know, we’re looking at all of the restaurants in the city which obviously is information that DOHMH maintains and, you know, historically can be a high violation industry, and all of our past targets going back years and years and years, every company we’ve ever investigated in the past also got a letter like that. And you know, as we hear from workers, you know, as the year goes on, we’ll be able to look and see, you know, did this company get a notice of the new laws? There’s absolutely no excuse not to be in compliance with the law.

And what type of outreach is agency doing particularly for small businesses that might not be aware of the new requirements? How

do we make sure that they are aware? What kind of outreach is happening in that regard?

This is a key priority for me. I spoke at the National Supermarket Association yesterday about this. We’ve held online seminars with small businesses. We’re also educating workers, but business education is key. We have a Deputy Commissioner for External Affairs here who can add more on these efforts.

Thank you. Madam Speaker, I think education is a core component of I think how DCWP wants to approach our work. As the Commissioner mentioned, we don’t play gotcha with our laws. We want to make sure we’re engaging with folks in an honest discussion. Besides these webinars and what we call DCWP 101 events with business associations and representatives, we also engage in direct outreach to businesses, both through our Community Affairs team, but also our enforcement team that offers what we call VIP inspections where they offer any new business a free educational inspection to help them understand what their obligations are. We reach thousands of businesses through these

efforts across the year, the calendar year, and it’s something we’re looking to build upon.
And how many staff do you have dedicated to enforcement around this topic?
I’m going to kick that to our Deputy Commissioner.

So, we actually have our investigators, attorneys and data scientists in the Office of Labor Policy and Standards working on all of our laws. So, our– not including the new lines we’ve just received, we have 54 people in OLPS who work on all of our laws. The biggest area of work for us is three-fold, paid safe and sick leave, which we’re now calling the Protected Time Off Law, the Fair Work Week Law, and the Delivery Worker Laws.

Moving to a new topic, the Fair Act and Housing Affordability. So, since the Fair Act took effect on June 11th, 2025, DCWP has received over 1,400 complaints related to illegal broker fees, but it appears only 50 summonses to real estate brokers, landlords or property managers have been filed which equates to roughly 3.5 percent of

total complaints. Can you explain why that is the case?

Yeah, I’m happy to, Madam Speaker. I’ll say briefly that we’re– since the Fair Act was enacted, we’re now up to 73 summons, $27,000 in penalties awarded by OATH, $15,000 awarded in restitution. But there’s still a gap as you recognized. The basis for that is two-fold, and our General Counsel can add more to this. One, sometimes we will get– often we will get complaints from folks who are not actually charged a broker fee, but maybe their friend told them they were charged a broker fee or they attempted to charge a broker fee. We will follow up. We will not always be able to follow up and actually reach that broker. So, part of it is just general awareness of the Fair Act, and we’re very proud of our outreach campaign on that. Part of that also is just the OATH process. A lot of these cases are moving through OATH and you are seeing the number of recoveries for consumers steadily rising. Mike, you want to add to that?

No, that’s absolutely right. We took– when this law came on board we took it very seriously and prioritized it,

and I think just to note, this new investment that the Commissioner was talking about by the Mamdani administration is definitely something we are going to– the Fair Act and other rental issues, the issues that arose during the Mayor’s Rental Rip Off hearings are definitely a topic that we are going to use when we get these new lines on board to redouble our efforts, especially for the Fair Act.

Okay. I want to switch gears to financial counseling, and then I’m going to pass it over to Chair Lee. So the percentage of DCWP financial counseling clients achieving a financial goal within their first year dropped from 21.1 percent in fiscal year 25 to 17.3 percent in fiscal year 26 which is the lowest rate in at least three years, and well below the agency’s directional target to improve this figure. The number of clients served also fell by six percent. Given the administration’s stated affordability agenda, what does the fiscal 2027 Executive Budget include specifically for this program, and what is driving the deteriorating outcome rates?

Yeah, well let me start by saying, financial empowerment centers serve

thousands of New Yorkers every year. You know, with respect to the outcomes on the MMR, the timeframe was shortened to a year. Many of our clients are looking for longer-term financial help where we just don’t have data. So not all of the benefits that our clients in the financial empowerment centers realize are– come through in that data because it’s a longer term estimate. As a general matter, though, Speaker, I completely agree. We want to get more New Yorkers using our financial empowerment centers. We have capacity. We have wonderful partners all over New York City. We want people getting– many of our staff have used these counselors, gotten outstanding results. We want more New Yorkers to benefit. In terms of the budget, I don’t know if you have that handy for financial empowerment. We are targeting an increase. It’s going to be FY26, it’s $4.8 million.

I would also– I appreciate the Commissioner’s point about our staff using our services. We’re very proud of the financial empowerment centers. We’ve even had two Commissioners that have had their student loan debt forgiven through our financial empowerment centres. Since inception we’ve increased our savings for New

Yorkers by $15.6 million and we helped reduce that by $135 million. So, it’s a fundamental program for the agency.
Okay. Alright. Thank you. I’m going to turn it over to– back to Chair Lee.
